title: A geometric relation of the error introduced by sampling a language model's output distribution to its internal state
claim: A single-token change at a high-entropy generation point sends a model's reasoning down a diverging path and changes its final answer.
layout: Chess board top-left, prompt beside it, then a diff-coloured completion below
description: A text-heavy figure with a chess board at top left and the prompt at top right. The board shows a mid-game position with a purple arrow on the b4 pawn and a crimson arrow from the b7 knight toward c5. The prompt asks the model to play White, think step by step and find the best move from a long PGN. Under it, 'Completion before branch' shows only the words 'Let's analyze the'. Below that is a 'Difference' section. It shows the model's analysis as a diff in which black text is shared, red bracketed text is deleted and teal text is new, until the word '[diverged]'. At the bottom, 'End of Completion' lists two different final recommendations: 19. b5 and 19. Nc5. The eye goes first to the board, then to the red and green diff text.
caption: Impact of single-token perturbation at position 4 on reasoning and final move recommendation. Shows the completion before branching and then the difference between the continuations. In the difference, black, red, and green colours indicate coinciding, deleted, and new text in the perturbed completions.
abstract: GPT-style language models are sensitive to single-token changes at generation points where the predicted probability distribution is spread across multiple tokens. Viewing this sensitivity as a geometric property, we derive an $\mathfrak{so}(n)$-valued 1-form that depends only on the geometry of the token embeddings. Despite this purely geometric origin, we show that its curvature is semantically meaningful: On chess reasoning tasks, the curvature couples to the world model of an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned model, with transformations clustering by board region and respecting piece importance. Our findings suggest that token space geometry directly reflects how models internally represent problems.
